questions.title: Deadlock Storm Under Load: Root Cause and Prevention
questions.prompt: Your OLTP system is throwing an increasing number of deadlock errors (1205) during peak hours, and the on-call team's current fix is just to retry the failed transaction. As the architect, walk through: what a deadlock actually is at the lock-manager level, why SQL Server resolves it by picking a victim, and the concrete, durable design changes you'd make to drive the deadlock rate toward zero rather than just making retries cheaper.
questions.modelAnswer: A deadlock is a circular wait: Transaction A holds a lock Transaction B needs, while B simultaneously holds a lock A needs, so neither can ever proceed without intervention. SQL Server's lock monitor periodically scans for exactly this cycle and, once found, picks a 'victim' to roll back automatically, based on which transaction is cheaper to undo (or an explicit DEADLOCK_PRIORITY setting), raising error 1205 to the victim's caller. Retrying the rolled-back transaction only treats the symptom — it does nothing to reduce how often the cycle forms in the first place. The durable fixes are architectural: (1) enforce a consistent access order to tables across every code path that touches them, since the single most common real-world cause is two transactions locking the same two tables in opposite order; (2) keep transactions as short as possible, moving validation and unrelated reads outside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary so locks are held for the minimum necessary time; (3) review indexing so transactions acquire narrow row/page locks instead of escalating to page or table locks on large scans, which dramatically widens the blast radius of any single transaction; (4) consider READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT isolation, which removes most reader/writer blocking entirely via row versioning, at the cost of additional tempdb version-store overhead; (5) for cases where natural ordering genuinely can't be enforced, use sp_getapplock to serialize access explicitly. Before declaring any fix complete, capture an actual deadlock graph (via Extended Events' xml_deadlock_report) to confirm the real access pattern rather than guessing from symptoms.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the team, respectfully, that retrying is a band-aid, not a fix — it just hides the real cost of the problem. First I'd pull an actual deadlock graph, not just the error count, because I want to see exactly which two statements and which two resources are colliding before I propose anything. Nine times out of ten it comes down to two code paths touching the same tables in opposite order, so step one is standardizing access order across every stored procedure that touches those tables. Step two is auditing transaction length — anything that's validating data or doing unrelated reads inside the BEGIN/COMMIT boundary comes out. Then I look at whether lock escalation is widening the blast radius because of missing indexes, and only after that do I bring up snapshot isolation as a structural option, being upfront that it moves the cost into tempdb rather than eliminating it. I'd present this as 'here's the mechanism, here's the evidence, here's what actually gets the rate toward zero' rather than just 'add a try/catch and retry.'
commonMistakes: Treats retry logic as the fix instead of eliminating the cause
Doesn't look at actual access order across stored procedures
Ignores lock escalation thresholds on large updates
Assumes deadlocks are a bug SQL Server should prevent rather than a resolvable mutual-wait
Never captures an actual deadlock graph (XML) before proposing a fix
keyPoints: Defines deadlock as a circular wait on locks, not a generic error
Explains SQL Server's victim-selection mechanism
Identifies inconsistent access order as the most common root cause
Proposes shortening transactions and reviewing indexing to reduce lock footprint
Considers snapshot isolation as an architectural lever, with its tradeoff (tempdb/version store)
Recommends instrumentation (deadlock graph / extended events) before declaring a fix

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains deadlock mechanics and victim selection
Identifies root-cause patterns (access order, long transactions, lock escalation)
Proposes durable architectural fixes, not just retry logic
Addresses tradeoffs of snapshot isolation or other mitigations

questions.title: Reporting Queries Are Blocking the Nightly Order Pipeline
questions.prompt: Business users running ad-hoc reports against the live OLTP database during business hours are intermittently blocking order-entry transactions, and vice versa. Compare the architectural options — read-committed snapshot isolation, a reporting replica, and query hints like NOLOCK — and recommend what you'd actually implement, including what you give up.
questions.modelAnswer: Under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level, readers take shared locks and writers take exclusive locks, so reports and order-entry transactions genuinely contend for the same locks on the same rows, causing exactly this symptom. NOLOCK (or READ UNCOMMITTED) removes that blocking by skipping locking entirely, but it allows dirty reads, can double-count or miss rows during a page split, and is unacceptable for anything a finance or operations team relies on for correctness — I would not recommend it as a general answer here. READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), enabled at the database level, gives readers a transactionally consistent versioned snapshot from tempdb's version store instead of taking shared locks, so reporting reads stop blocking writers and vice versa, with zero application code changes for ordinary SELECTs — the cost is additional tempdb space and I/O for the version store, and a small per-row overhead on writers. A reporting replica (an Always On readable secondary, log shipping, or replication) solves a different, broader problem: it isolates the reporting workload's CPU and I/O consumption from the OLTP instance entirely, not just lock contention, at the cost of replication lag and additional infrastructure to maintain. My recommendation: enable RCSI first as the fast, low-risk fix for the specific symptom described (lock contention), and treat a readable secondary as the real architectural answer once the reporting workload itself starts consuming OLTP compute/I/O capacity, not just locks. The two aren't mutually exclusive — a mature design often has both.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd separate this into two different problems that look the same from the outside: lock contention, and resource contention. For the immediate symptom — reports and order entry fighting over row locks — I'd recommend turning on read-committed snapshot isolation. It lets readers work off a versioned snapshot instead of taking shared locks, so the blocking just stops, and it needs no code changes. I'd be upfront that it's not free — it adds load to tempdb's version store — but that's a much safer tradeoff than reaching for NOLOCK, which I'd actually argue against here, because dirty reads on order data are a real correctness risk, not just a theoretical one. If the real issue turns out to be that reporting is also eating CPU and I/O the OLTP system needs, that's a different conversation — that's when I'd bring in a readable secondary, because RCSI doesn't give you more hardware, it just removes lock contention. I'd frame it to the client as 'quick structural fix now, workload separation as the next step if reporting keeps growing.'
commonMistakes: Recommends NOLOCK as a general-purpose fix without flagging dirty-read risk
Doesn't distinguish lock contention from resource (CPU/IO) contention
Treats RCSI as free, ignoring tempdb version-store cost
Proposes a replica without acknowledging replication lag implications for 'real-time' reports
keyPoints: Explains why READ COMMITTED causes reader/writer blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and correctly rejects it for anything requiring correctness
Explains RCSI's row-versioning mechanism and its tempdb cost
Recommends a readable secondary/replica as the durable architecture for resource isolation
Distinguishes lock contention from compute contention

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the locking behavior causing the blocking
Evaluates NOLOCK and its risks accurately
Explains RCSI/snapshot isolation mechanism and cost
Recommends and justifies an appropriate architecture (replica vs RCSI)

questions.title: A Stored Procedure Is Recompiling Constantly Under Load
questions.prompt: A heavily-used stored procedure builds a large intermediate result set using a table variable, then joins it twice more inside the same procedure. Under load, you're seeing wildly inconsistent execution times and plan cache bloat. Diagnose why the table variable choice is likely the architectural root cause at this scale, and rewrite the approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Table variables historically carry no real statistics — on many compatibility levels the optimizer assumes roughly one row regardless of actual size — so when the intermediate set is genuinely large, the optimizer builds a plan sized for one row: an undersized memory grant and a join strategy that's wrong for the real row count. The inconsistent timing comes from actual row counts varying run to run while the cached plan was compiled against that wrong, fixed assumption, so some executions get lucky and others spill to disk or pick a bad join type. A #temp table, by contrast, gets real statistics maintained by SQL Server, letting the optimizer size the plan for the two downstream joins accurately. The tradeoff: a significant change in a temp table's row count can trigger a recompile — but that's a feature here, not a bug, since it means the plan adapts to actual data instead of staying wrong. The fix is to replace the DECLARE @T TABLE with a CREATE TABLE #T, optionally indexed if the joins warrant it, keeping the rest of the procedure's logic unchanged.
questions.professionalAnswer: What's happening here is that the optimizer doesn't have real numbers to work with. A table variable, on most compatibility levels, gets treated as roughly one row no matter how big it actually gets, so the plan built for it is sized for the wrong workload — that's exactly why the timing is inconsistent: the actual row count varies, but the plan doesn't adapt. My fix is to swap it for a #temp table, because SQL Server maintains real statistics on those, so the two downstream joins get a plan that's actually shaped for the data. I'll be upfront that this trades one problem for a different, much smaller one — a temp table can trigger a recompile when its row count shifts significantly — but I'd rather have an occasional recompile that produces a correct plan than a stable plan that's confidently wrong every time.
questions.example:
-- Before: table variable, optimizer assumes ~1 row
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    DECLARE @ActiveOrders TABLE (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    INSERT INTO @ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM @ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO

-- After: temp table, real statistics, optionally indexed
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetRegionalSalesSummary
AS
BEGIN
    CREATE TABLE #ActiveOrders (OrderID INT, CustomerID INT, Amount MONEY);
    CREATE INDEX IX_ActiveOrders_CustomerID ON #ActiveOrders (CustomerID);

    INSERT INTO #ActiveOrders
    SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, Amount FROM dbo.Orders WHERE Status = 'Active';

    SELECT c.Region, SUM(a.Amount)
    FROM #ActiveOrders a
    JOIN dbo.Customers c ON c.CustomerID = a.CustomerID
    GROUP BY c.Region;
END
GO
commonMistakes: Treats 'table variables are always faster' as a universal rule
Doesn't connect inconsistent timing to missing statistics on a large table variable
Recommends a CTE instead, missing that a CTE is re-evaluated/inlined and doesn't solve the cardinality problem either
Adds an index to the table variable via inline constraint without recognizing its limits
Ignores the recompile tradeoff when switching to a temp table
keyPoints: Explains the statistics difference between table variables and temp tables
Connects missing statistics to bad cardinality estimation and inconsistent plans at scale
Chooses #temp table over table variable or CTE for this specific large, multiply-joined scenario
Provides a correct before/after rewrite
Acknowledges the recompile tradeoff as acceptable here

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses missing statistics as the root cause
Chooses the right replacement structure with justification
Provides correct, working SQL example
Acknowledges tradeoffs (recompilation) honestly

questions.title: Parameter Sniffing: One Cached Plan, Two Very Different Row Counts
questions.prompt: A stored procedure filters orders by @CustomerID. For a customer with a handful of orders it returns in milliseconds; for your biggest customer with several million rows, the exact same procedure call times out. Nothing about the query changed. Explain what's actually happening at the plan-cache level, and lay out the durable fixes you'd choose between, including the tradeoffs of each.
questions.modelAnswer: This is parameter sniffing: when a stored procedure compiles, SQL Server peeks at the actual parameter value supplied on that first call and builds one cached execution plan optimized for that value's estimated row count, then reuses that same plan for every subsequent call regardless of what parameter comes in next. If the plan was compiled against a small customer, the optimizer chose a plan shaped for a small result set — likely nested loops with a lookup — and that same plan is catastrophic against a customer with millions of rows, where a hash or merge join with a full scan would have been far cheaper. The symptom isn't random; it's entirely a function of which value happened to compile the plan, which is why it looks like it 'used to work.' Durable fixes, in order of how I'd actually choose: (1) OPTION (RECOMPILE) on the statement forces a fresh, value-specific plan on every execution — correct for every call, but pays the compilation cost every single time, which is wasteful for a high-frequency procedure; (2) OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR @CustomerID UNKNOWN) tells the optimizer to use the average-distribution estimate instead of sniffing any single value, which avoids the worst-case outlier plan but may make the common case slightly less optimal; (3) WITH RECOMPILE at the procedure level has the same cost profile as per-statement recompile but applies to the whole procedure; (4) query store plan forcing lets you pin a known-good plan once you've identified one that performs acceptably across the real distribution of parameter values, which is a strong operational fix but needs monitoring since data growth can eventually make the forced plan wrong too; (5) splitting the procedure into two paths (a small-customer branch and a large-customer branch, chosen by an IF before the query even runs) avoids a single plan ever having to serve both distributions, at the cost of more code to maintain. I'd pick based on call frequency and skew: for a rarely-called heavy procedure, RECOMPILE is cheap enough; for a hot-path procedure called thousands of times a minute, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN or query store plan forcing is usually the right call, because paying a full recompile on every call would itself become the bottleneck.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through it the same way I'd explain it to the team that paged me: the procedure didn't change, the data behind one parameter value did, and the plan cache is still serving a plan that was shaped for a tiny customer. SQL Server only looks at the parameter value once, on the first compile, and then it's locked in until something invalidates that plan. So the fix isn't 'optimize the query' — the query's fine — it's deciding how we want the optimizer to handle that skew going forward. For something called rarely, I'd just slap OPTION (RECOMPILE) on it and move on, because paying for a fresh plan every call is cheap compared to how rarely it runs. For something hot, I don't want to recompile constantly, so I'd reach for OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN first, which tells the optimizer to plan for the average case instead of gambling on whichever value shows up first — and if I need something more surgical, I'll go find a known-good plan and force it through Query Store, which I'll then keep an eye on, because a forced plan isn't a fix I set once and forget; the data keeps growing underneath it.
commonMistakes: Describes the symptom (it's slow for one customer) without naming the plan-cache mechanism causing it
Jumps straight to adding an index without addressing that a single cached plan is the root cause
Recommends OPTION (RECOMPILE) everywhere without weighing its per-call compilation cost on hot paths
Doesn't mention Query Store plan forcing as an operational option
Treats the fix as permanent without noting that data growth can make a forced or optimized-for plan wrong again later
keyPoints: Correctly explains that one parameter value's estimate shapes the cached plan for all future calls
Distinguishes RECOMPILE (per-call cost, always-correct plan) from OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN (average-case plan, no per-call cost)
Mentions Query Store plan forcing as a monitored, surgical fix
Considers call frequency and data skew when choosing between the options
Notes that any chosen fix needs to be revisited as data distribution changes over time

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the parameter-sniffing / plan-cache mechanism
Presents multiple durable fixes (RECOMPILE, OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, Query Store forcing, branching)
Weighs the real tradeoffs (per-call cost vs. plan quality) rather than naming one fix blindly
Chooses between fixes based on call frequency / skew, not a one-size-fits-all answer

questions.title: Fix a Non-SARGable, Non-Covering Query Under Load
questions.prompt:
You're handed this production query that's doing a full clustered index scan on a 40-million-row table, confirmed via SET STATISTICS IO showing logical reads in the hundreds of thousands:

SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) = '06/15/2013'
   AND UPPER(Status) = 'SHIPPED';

Rewrite the query to be SARGable, and write the covering index you'd create to support it, explaining your column order choice.
questions.modelAnswer: There are two non-SARGable predicates here, and both need fixing. CONVERT(VARCHAR(10), OrderDate, 101) wraps the date column in a function, forcing a scan even if an index exists; UPPER(Status) does the same to the status column. The date predicate should be rewritten as a half-open range against the raw column; the status predicate should compare against the literal in its natural case, relying on the column's collation to be case-insensitive rather than forcing a transformation on every row. For the covering index, the equality predicate (Status) should lead the key, since equality columns belong before range columns in a composite index — this lets SQL Server seek to the exact Status value, then scan only the OrderDate range within that narrower slice — and the remaining selected columns go into INCLUDE so the plan never needs a Key Lookup back to the clustered index.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out there are actually two separate problems stacked in that one WHERE clause, not one. The CONVERT around OrderDate and the UPPER around Status are both doing the same damage — wrapping the column so the index can't be used no matter how well it's built. I'd rewrite the date as a range against the raw column and drop the UPPER, trusting the collation to handle case. Then for the index, I always put the equality column first — Status — because that lets SQL Server narrow down to an exact value before it even has to think about the date range, and I'd include the rest of the selected columns so we get a fully covering seek with no extra trip back to the clustered index.
questions.example:
-- SARGable rewrite
SELECT OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TotalDue
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader
WHERE Status = 'Shipped'
  AND OrderDate >= '2013-06-15' AND OrderDate < '2013-06-16';

-- Covering index: equality column first, then the range column, then INCLUDE the rest
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_SalesOrderHeader_Status_OrderDate
ON Sales.SalesOrderHeader (Status, OrderDate)
INCLUDE (OrderID, CustomerID, TotalDue);
commonMistakes: Only fixes one of the two non-SARGable predicates
Puts the range column before the equality column in the index key
Forgets INCLUDE columns, leaving a Key Lookup in the plan
Assumes UPPER() is needed without checking the column's collation
keyPoints: Identifies both non-SARGable predicates
Rewrites the date predicate as a range
Removes the function wrapper on Status, citing collation
Designs index key order correctly: equality before range
Makes the index covering with INCLUDE

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly rewrites both non-SARGable predicates
Index design uses correct key order (equality before range)
Index is fully covering via INCLUDE
Explains reasoning, not just the syntax

lessonLink.label: Review: SARGable vs. Non-SARGable WHERE Clauses

questions.title: Find the Head of a Live Blocking Chain
questions.prompt: Users are reporting the application is frozen. You suspect blocking, not an outage. Write the T-SQL you'd run right now against the live server to find the head blocker — the session that isn't waiting on anyone else but is blocking everyone downstream — and explain what you'd do with the session ID once you have it.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd query sys.dm_exec_requests joined to sys.dm_exec_sessions, filtering for sessions that have a non-zero blocking_session_id to see everyone currently blocked, then specifically look for the blocking_session_id value that does not itself appear as a session_id with its own non-zero blocking_session_id — that session is the head blocker, the one actually holding the lock everyone else is waiting on. Once I have it, I'd pull its current or last statement via sys.dm_exec_sql_text and check open_tran_count and last_request_start_time to understand what it's actually doing and how long it's been doing it, rather than acting blind. Only if it's clearly stuck or abnormally long-running would I consider KILLing the session, understanding that the kill itself rolls back its transaction and can take as long or longer than letting it finish. The real fix afterward is to find out why that session held locks so long — a missing index causing a slow scan while holding a write lock, or application code that doesn't commit promptly — because KILL is an emergency release valve, not a repeatable procedure.
questions.professionalAnswer: When I hear 'the app is frozen,' my first move is never to panic and start killing sessions — it's to find out if this is actually blocking, and if so, where it starts. I'd run a query against dm_exec_requests joined to dm_exec_sessions, filtering for anyone currently blocked, and then specifically look for the one session that's blocking others but isn't itself waiting on anyone — that's my head blocker. Before I touch it, I want to know what it's actually running and how long it's been running it, because killing it rolls back its transaction, and that rollback can take just as long as letting it finish. Once things are stable again, the real work starts: finding out why that session held locks that long in the first place, because if I don't fix that, I'm back here again next week.
questions.example:
SELECT 
    r.session_id,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.status,
    s.login_name,
    s.host_name,
    t.text AS running_sql
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s ON s.session_id = r.session_id
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) AS t
WHERE r.session_id IN (
    SELECT blocking_session_id FROM sys.dm_exec_requests WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0
)
AND r.blocking_session_id = 0;  -- the head blocker: blocking others, blocked by no one
commonMistakes: Immediately KILLs a session without identifying the actual head blocker first
Confuses a long-running query with a blocking chain — not every slow query is blocking others
Doesn't capture what the head blocker's own transaction was doing before acting
Treats sp_who2 output alone as sufficient without the actual SQL text or wait info
keyPoints: Correctly identifies the head-blocker query pattern using DMVs
Explains the difference between being blocked and being the source of blocking
Describes a safe escalation path (investigate before KILL)
Connects the fix back to root cause (missing index, long transaction, app behavior)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working query identifying the head blocker
Explains the DMV logic clearly
Describes a safe, sensible escalation/response procedure
Connects to durable root-cause fix, not just killing sessions

questions.title: Replace a Row-by-Row Price Update With a Set-Based Rewrite
questions.prompt: A nightly job uses a cursor to apply a different percentage increase to ListPrice per product category, reading category-specific rates from a rates table. It takes 40 minutes against 2 million products. Rewrite it as a single set-based statement.
questions.modelAnswer: The cursor's cost comes from processing one row at a time — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, each with its own overhead, multiplied by two million. SQL Server's storage engine is built to process sets of rows efficiently, so the fix is to express the same logic as a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, letting the engine apply the whole operation at once instead of looping. I'd use ISNULL to handle any product whose subcategory has no matching rate, so it's left unchanged rather than silently zeroed out by a NULL multiplication. I'd check that the join column is indexed before declaring victory, and only consider batching the update (e.g., with TOP(n) in a loop) if the single statement itself causes problematic lock duration or transaction log growth at this volume — I wouldn't reach for batching as the first move.
questions.professionalAnswer: Forty minutes for two million rows is a huge tell that something's being processed one row at a time, and sure enough, that's exactly what the cursor is doing — a fetch, a lookup, and an update per product, over and over. My rewrite is a single UPDATE joined to the rates table, because that lets the storage engine do what it's actually built for, which is operating on a whole set at once instead of looping. The one detail I wouldn't skip is handling products whose subcategory has no matching rate — I use a LEFT JOIN with ISNULL so those rows just stay unchanged instead of silently getting multiplied by a NULL. And I'd check the join column has an index before I call this done, because a 40-minute cursor sometimes hides a missing index underneath it too.
commonMistakes: Keeps per-row logic inside a WHILE loop over a temp table, which is just a hand-rolled cursor
Forgets to handle categories with no matching rate row (NULL rate silently zeroing the increase)
Doesn't check whether the join column is indexed before declaring victory
Jumps to batching/chunking as the first solution instead of trying the plain set-based statement first
keyPoints: Correctly diagnoses the cursor as the core bottleneck, not server hardware
Produces a correct, equivalent set-based UPDATE...FROM
Handles the no-matching-rate case correctly (ISNULL or join behavior)
Considers indexing and batching only as secondary, scale-driven refinements

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses cursor overhead as root cause
Produces a correct, working set-based rewrite
Handles edge cases (no matching rate) correctly
Discusses sensible secondary considerations (indexing, batching) without over-engineering

questions.title: Nightly Load and Morning Reports Are Deadlocking Each Other
questions.prompt: The nightly ETL load now runs long enough to overlap with early-morning reporting queries, and you're seeing a spike in deadlock errors (1205) exactly in that overlap window. Write the query you'd use to capture the actual deadlock graphs (not just the error count), and describe the architectural fix once you've confirmed the access pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: SQL Server Profiler is deprecated, so I'd capture real deadlock graphs through Extended Events — either reading the always-on system_health session's xml_deadlock_report, or standing up a dedicated session — and extract the XML to see exactly which two statements and which objects/lock modes were involved. That turns 'we have deadlocks' into a concrete finding, like 'the ETL's bulk insert into FactOrderSales and a reporting SELECT doing a range scan are colliding on the same rows.' Once that's confirmed, I'd rank the fix options by durability: first, enable READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT so reporting SELECTs stop taking the shared locks that participate in the deadlock at all, which addresses it structurally rather than by luck of timing; second, shrink and restructure the ETL's transactions so they hold locks for the shortest possible time and touch narrower row ranges, through smaller batches or partition-aligned loads; third, if this keeps recurring, separate the workloads architecturally — widen or shift the load window, or move reporting onto a readable secondary — so the two workloads stop contending for the same locks on the same instance entirely. I'd recommend RCSI as the fast structural win and workload separation as the long-term answer if the overlap keeps growing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't propose a fix off an error count alone — I want the actual deadlock graph first, so I'm pulling it from the system_health Extended Events session rather than reaching for Profiler, which is deprecated at this point. Once I can see exactly which two statements and which rows are colliding, I can say something specific, like 'the nightly bulk insert and a reporting range scan are fighting over the same rows,' instead of just 'we have deadlocks.' From there, my go-to structural fix is read-committed snapshot isolation, because it takes the reporting side out of the locking picture entirely instead of just making it less likely to collide. If the client's really pushing both workloads hard, I'd also talk about shrinking the ETL's transactions and, longer term, moving reporting to a readable secondary — but I'd never reach for NOLOCK as the answer here, because trading a deadlock for a dirty read isn't actually a fix.
questions.example:
-- Query system_health's ring buffer for recent deadlock graphs
SELECT
    xed.value('(event/@timestamp)[1]', 'datetime2') AS EventTime,
    xed.query('.') AS DeadlockGraph
FROM sys.fn_xe_file_target_read_file('system_health*.xel', NULL, NULL, NULL) AS f
CROSS APPLY (SELECT CAST(f.event_data AS XML) AS xed) AS d
WHERE xed.value('(event/@name)[1]', 'varchar(100)') = 'xml_deadlock_report'
ORDER BY EventTime DESC;
commonMistakes: Tries to diagnose deadlocks from just the error count/frequency instead of capturing the actual graph
Jumps straight to NOLOCK on the reporting queries as a 'fix', reintroducing dirty-read risk
Only addresses the symptom (overlap timing) without checking whether RCSI would remove the lock conflict structurally
Recommends a replica without first confirming the deadlock is lock-contention, not resource-contention
keyPoints: Uses Extended Events (not deprecated Profiler) to capture real deadlock graphs
Translates the captured graph into a concrete statement-level root cause before proposing a fix
Evaluates RCSI as a structural fix for reader/writer lock conflicts
Considers transaction shrinkage and workload separation (replica) as complementary long-term fixes
Avoids NOLOCK as a quick-fix answer

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct approach to capturing real deadlock graph evidence
Correctly reasons from captured evidence to root cause
Proposes RCSI or equivalent structural fix with justification
Considers workload separation/transaction design as durable long-term fix

questions.title: A Report Query That Used to Run in 2 Seconds Now Takes Over a Minute
questions.prompt: A nightly report query filtering orders by date has gone from roughly 2 seconds to over a minute as the Orders table grew past 40 million rows. The WHERE clause uses a function on the indexed OrderDate column to normalize it before comparing. Nobody changed the query text or the index. Walk through your diagnostic sequence and provide the corrected query.
questions.modelAnswer: First I'd pull the actual execution plan (not estimated) for the query and check whether it's doing an Index Seek or a Scan on OrderDate — on a 40M-row table, a scan where a seek should be possible is the key signal. The WHERE clause wraps the indexed column in CONVERT(date, OrderDate), and applying a function to the column itself makes the predicate non-SARGable: SQL Server can't use the index's sorted order to seek, because it would have to evaluate CONVERT() against every row's OrderDate before it even knows which rows match, forcing a full scan. This likely always technically had this issue, but it only became painfully visible once the table grew enough that scanning became expensive — small tables hide non-SARGable predicates because a full scan is cheap when there's little data. Fix: rewrite the predicate to leave the column bare and move the transformation to the literal side, using a range comparison instead of transforming OrderDate: WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-10-08' AND OrderDate < '2026-10-09'. This lets the optimizer seek directly against the OrderDate index. I'd confirm the fix by re-checking the execution plan for an Index Seek and comparing logical reads/duration before and after.
questions.professionalAnswer: I don't start by looking at the index or assuming it got dropped or fragmented — I go get the actual execution plan first, because 'nothing changed' usually means the query had a latent problem the whole time that only became expensive once the table crossed some size. And sure enough, the plan shows a full scan on a 40-million-row table even though there's an index sitting right there on OrderDate. The WHERE clause is the giveaway: CONVERT(date, OrderDate) = '...' wraps the indexed column in a function, and the moment you do that, the optimizer can't use the index's sort order to seek — it has to convert every single row before it can compare anything, so a scan is the only option it has left. This bug was there on day one, it just didn't matter when the table was small enough that a full scan was basically free; growth is what exposed it, not a change to the query or index. The fix is just to stop touching the column and instead express the same filter as a range against the raw OrderDate value — greater than or equal to midnight on the target day, less than midnight the next day — so the predicate stays SARGable and the optimizer can seek straight to the right rows. I make the change, pull the plan again, confirm it's an Index Seek now, and compare logical reads before and after so I have real numbers to point to, not just 'it feels faster.'

Not pulling the actual execution plan and instead guessing based on query text alone
Rebuilding or adding indexes without first fixing the function-wrapped predicate that prevents any index from being seek-able
Fixing it by wrapping the literal in the same function (CONVERT on both sides) instead of removing the function from the column side entirely
Not validating the fix by comparing before/after execution plans or logical reads
Blaming table growth alone as 'just needs more hardware' instead of identifying the specific non-SARGable predicate

Correctly identifies the function-wrapped column as the SARGability problem
Explains why this was a latent issue exposed by growth rather than a new regression

Confirms the fix via execution plan (Index Seek) and reads/duration comparison
Understands that the index itself was never the problem

questions.title: Prioritizing a Backlog of Competing Dashboard Requests
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time you had a large backlog of dashboard and report requests from multiple departments, all claiming urgency. How did you build a prioritization framework and communicate it back to stakeholders?
questions.modelAnswer: The answer should quantify the backlog problem — number of open requests, number of competing departments, and why 'everything is urgent' had become the default. It should describe a concrete prioritization framework rather than ad hoc judgment calls: scoring requests against criteria like business impact, number of downstream decisions affected, cost of delay, and build effort, and making that framework visible to requesters rather than opaque. It should show how the framework was communicated back to stakeholders whose requests ranked lower — specifically how the candidate avoided just disappointing people silently, by explaining the reasoning and giving a realistic timeline. Strong answers mention a lightweight intake and triage process (a backlog board, a regular grooming cadence) so prioritization becomes repeatable rather than a one-time exercise, and close with a measurable outcome: reduced average time-to-delivery, fewer 'why hasn't my request been touched' escalations, or higher stakeholder satisfaction with transparency even when their request wasn't first in line.
questions.professionalAnswer: I inherited a backlog of 47 open dashboard requests across six departments, each department insisting theirs was the most urgent, with no shared criteria for sequencing any of it. I built a simple scoring model with four weighted factors — number of people who'd use it regularly, whether it supported a recurring decision versus a one-off curiosity, estimated build effort, and cost of continuing to delay it — and scored every open request against it in a spreadsheet I made visible to all six department leads, not just my own team. I ran a 30-minute session with each lead to walk through how their specific requests scored and why, which let me say 'your request is real and matters, here's exactly where it lands and why' instead of a vague 'we'll get to it.' Two leads pushed back hard on their ranking, and in one case they were right — I'd underweighted a compliance-driven request from Legal that had a hard regulatory deadline I hadn't accounted for, so I added a deadline-override factor to the model. We moved to a visible Kanban board with a biweekly grooming session so this became routine instead of a one-time fire drill. Average time from request to delivery dropped from eleven weeks to under four, and escalations to my manager about 'my request is stuck' dropped to nearly zero because people could see exactly where they stood and why.
commonMistakes: No concrete scoring criteria, just 'we prioritized based on urgency'
Keeping the prioritization logic opaque instead of sharing it with requesters
Not addressing how deprioritized stakeholders were communicated with
Treating the first prioritization pass as final instead of being open to correction
No repeatable process established, just a one-time cleanup
No measurable improvement in delivery time or stakeholder satisfaction

questions.title: Explaining Self-Attention to a Skeptical Stakeholder Who Thinks It's a Black Box
questions.prompt: A senior stakeholder who approved budget for an LLM-based feature says they 'don't trust a black box' and wants a real explanation of how a transformer actually decides what matters in a sentence, not a marketing analogy. Walk through self-attention and multi-head attention mechanically, and explain why this architecture replaced RNNs for most NLP work.
questions.modelAnswer: Self-attention computes, for every token in a sequence, a weighted combination of every other token's representation, where the weights are learned relevance scores rather than fixed positions. Mechanically, each token's embedding is projected into three vectors — Query, Key, and Value — via learned weight matrices. The attention score between token i and token j is the dot product of i's Query and j's Key, scaled by the square root of the key dimension to keep gradients stable, then passed through softmax across all j so the scores sum to 1. Each token's new representation is the weighted sum of all Value vectors using those softmax weights, meaning a token like 'it' can pull context directly from a noun many words earlier without having to pass information through every intermediate word, the way a recurrent network would. Multi-head attention runs several of these Query/Key/Value projections in parallel with different learned weights, so one head can specialize in syntactic relationships (subject-verb agreement) while another tracks coreference or topical relevance, and their outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension. This replaced RNNs for two concrete reasons: RNNs process tokens sequentially, so a dependency between word 1 and word 500 has to survive 499 compounding transformations, which is where vanishing gradients and lost long-range context come from; transformers compute all pairwise relationships in one matrix multiplication, so long-range dependencies are just as cheap as short ones, and the whole sequence can be processed in parallel on a GPU instead of token-by-token, which is also why transformers scale so much better with more data and compute.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip the black-box framing entirely and just open the hood. I'd tell them: for every word, the model computes how relevant every other word is to it, using three learned vectors per word — a Query, a Key, and a Value. You multiply Query against Key to get a relevance score, normalize those scores with softmax so they act like percentages, and then blend the Value vectors using those percentages. That's it — that's attention. Multi-head just means the model does this several times in parallel with different learned lenses, so one 'head' might end up tracking grammar while another tracks which noun a pronoun refers to, and we concatenate those views back together. The reason this replaced RNNs isn't fashion — RNNs have to pass information through every single word in order, so a connection between word 1 and word 500 has to survive 499 hops and usually doesn't. Attention lets word 500 look directly at word 1 in one step, and because it's all matrix multiplication instead of a sequential loop, it runs in parallel on a GPU, which is also exactly why these models could be scaled up as far as they have been. I'd finish by saying: it's not unexplainable, it's just linear algebra applied consistently — the 'black box' feeling usually comes from the model being very large, not from the mechanism being mysterious.
commonMistakes: Describes attention only as an analogy ('the model focuses on important words') without the Query/Key/Value mechanics
Forgets the softmax normalization step or the scaling factor and why it matters for gradient stability
Treats multi-head attention as just 'more attention' without explaining that each head learns a different relationship
Can't articulate the concrete RNN limitation (sequential dependency, vanishing gradients over distance) that attention solves
Conflates attention with the entire transformer block, ignoring feed-forward layers and residual connections
keyPoints: Explains Query/Key/Value projections and the dot-product/softmax scoring mechanism
Explains multi-head attention as parallel, differently-specialized attention computations
Connects the mechanism to why long-range dependencies are cheap in transformers
Explains the concrete RNN limitation (sequential processing, vanishing gradients) being solved
Delivers the explanation in a way a non-technical stakeholder can actually follow

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the Query/Key/Value self-attention mechanism
Correctly explains multi-head attention
Accurately contrasts with RNN limitations
Communicates clearly to a non-technical stakeholder

questions.title: Prompting vs. Fine-Tuning vs. RAG: Choosing the Right Lever
questions.prompt: Leadership keeps asking 'why don't we just fine-tune our own model instead of paying for API calls?' Explain the real differences between prompting, fine-tuning, and retrieval-augmented generation as ways to adapt an LLM to a domain, and give the decision framework you'd use to choose between them for a given use case.
questions.modelAnswer: These three operate at different layers and solve different problems, and conflating them is the most common strategic mistake in this space. Prompting adapts behavior at inference time through instructions, few-shot examples, or structured output requests, with zero training cost and instant iteration, but it's bounded by the model's existing knowledge and the context window — it can't teach the model new facts it never saw, and it re-pays the context cost on every call. Fine-tuning updates the model's weights on a labeled dataset of input/output examples, which is the right tool for teaching a consistent style, format, or task-specific behavior (classification, structured extraction, a particular tone) that you can demonstrate with enough examples — it is not an efficient way to inject large volumes of fast-changing factual knowledge, because every data update requires a retraining cycle, and it carries real cost in data curation, compute, and evaluation. RAG keeps the base model's weights frozen and instead retrieves relevant documents at query time from an external knowledge store, injecting them into the prompt as context — this is the right tool when the need is 'answer correctly about our constantly-changing internal data' rather than 'behave in a specific stylistic way,' because updating the knowledge base is just re-indexing documents, not retraining a model, and answers can cite their sources. My decision framework: if the problem is about teaching a task/format/behavior, fine-tune; if the problem is about keeping answers grounded in current, large, or proprietary knowledge, use RAG; if the problem is solvable by giving better instructions or examples within the existing capability of the model, prompt first because it's the cheapest and fastest to validate. In practice, most production systems combine prompting and RAG, and reach for fine-tuning only when prompting and RAG both plateau on a task the model fundamentally doesn't do well.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd answer the 'why not fine-tune' question by reframing it: fine-tuning isn't a replacement for API calls, it's a different tool solving a different problem. If what we need is the model to answer questions grounded in our own, constantly-changing documentation, fine-tuning is actually the wrong tool — every time our docs change we'd have to retrain, which is slow and expensive, whereas RAG just means re-indexing a document store, and we get source citations for free. Fine-tuning earns its cost when we need the model to reliably do a specific task in a specific format over and over — think structured extraction or a consistent voice — where we can demonstrate that behavior with a solid set of labeled examples. And before either of those, I always ask whether better prompting alone gets us there, because it costs nothing to try and we learn fast whether the model's base capability is even sufficient. I'd walk leadership through it as a ladder: try prompting first, add RAG when the problem is about grounding in our own knowledge, and only fine-tune when we have a stable, repeatable task with enough labeled data to make retraining worth the ongoing maintenance cost.
commonMistakes: Treats fine-tuning as a general knowledge-injection method rather than a behavior/format-adaptation method
Doesn't mention that RAG keeps the base model frozen and works by injecting retrieved context
Ignores the ongoing maintenance cost difference (re-indexing vs. retraining) when data changes
Jumps straight to fine-tuning without considering cheaper prompting iterations first
Doesn't provide an actual decision framework, just lists the three options

Identifies fine-tuning's strength (consistent task/format/behavior) and weakness (poor fit for fast-changing facts)
Identifies RAG's strength (grounding in current/large knowledge, source citation) and its retrieval-quality dependency
Gives a clear, usable decision framework rather than a neutral list

questions.title: Tokenization and Context Windows at Scale: Why the Bill and the Behavior Both Depend on It
questions.prompt: A product manager wants to know why the same user question sometimes costs more to send to an LLM API than other times, and why the model 'forgets' things said earlier in a long conversation. Explain tokenization and context windows at a level that justifies both observations, including the practical implications for a system processing high volumes of enterprise documents.
questions.modelAnswer: LLMs don't process characters or whole words directly — text is first split into tokens by a subword tokenizer (commonly byte-pair encoding or a variant), where common words might be a single token but rarer words, unusual formatting, or non-English text can fragment into several tokens each. This is exactly why cost varies per request: API pricing is per token, not per character or per request, so a question full of technical jargon, code, or non-English text can cost noticeably more than a similarly-long plain-English question, because it tokenizes into more pieces. The context window is the fixed maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in a single call, covering the system prompt, any retrieved context, the conversation history, and the model's own output combined — once the running total approaches that limit, something has to be dropped or summarized, which is why a model appears to 'forget' earlier parts of a long conversation: it isn't forgetting, the earlier turns have literally fallen outside the window or been truncated by whatever context-management logic the application uses. At enterprise document-processing volume, both facts become operational constraints rather than trivia: token counts must be estimated and budgeted before sending a batch of documents, chunking strategy for long documents needs to respect the context window with room left for the prompt and output, and conversation-heavy applications need an explicit strategy — sliding window, summarization of older turns, or retrieval instead of raw history — because naively appending every turn will eventually either break the budget or silently drop content the user assumed the model still had.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it with the actual mechanism rather than a shortcut. The model doesn't see words, it sees tokens — chunks that a tokenizer breaks text into, and the chunking isn't uniform. Plain English words are often one token each, but jargon, code, or other languages can split into several tokens per word, and since the API bills per token, that's exactly why two questions that look the same length to a human can cost differently. On the 'forgetting' question, every model has a hard ceiling on how many tokens it can look at in one call — that's the context window, and it includes everything: the instructions, any retrieved documents, the whole conversation so far, and the response it's about to generate. Once a long conversation gets close to that ceiling, the application has to start dropping or compressing older turns to make room, so what looks like the model forgetting is really the application running out of room and making a choice about what to keep. For a system handling a lot of enterprise documents, I'd tell the PM this isn't a detail to wave away — we need to actually estimate token counts before we chunk documents or design conversation history handling, because getting this wrong either blows the budget or silently drops content a user is relying on.

questions.title: What Embeddings Actually Encode, and Why Cosine Similarity Is the Default Metric
questions.prompt: A colleague asks why you'd bother converting text to embeddings instead of just matching on keywords, and why cosine similarity specifically is used to compare them instead of a simpler distance measure. Give a technically grounded answer.
questions.modelAnswer: An embedding is a dense numeric vector produced by a model trained so that semantically similar inputs end up close together in that vector space, even when they share no words in common — 'the car wouldn't start' and 'my vehicle won't turn on' map to nearby vectors because the model learned meaning-based structure during training, not surface-level token overlap. Keyword matching can only find lexical overlap, so it structurally misses synonyms, paraphrases, and cross-lingual matches, which is precisely the gap embeddings close. On the metric choice: cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude, which matters because many embedding models produce vectors whose length correlates with factors like text length or token frequency rather than semantic strength — if you used Euclidean distance directly, a long, verbose but topically-unrelated document could score deceptively close to a short, highly relevant one simply because of vector-length effects. Cosine similarity isolates direction, which is what actually encodes meaning in these models, and because many embedding models are trained with a contrastive objective that directly optimizes cosine similarity between related pairs, using that same metric at retrieval time is consistent with how the representations were learned. In practice, when embeddings are L2-normalized ahead of time, cosine similarity and dot product become equivalent and computationally cheaper, which is why most production vector databases normalize vectors at ingestion and then use a dot-product index under the hood while still calling it 'cosine similarity' conceptually.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start with the actual gap keyword search leaves open: it can only find text that shares words, so it misses 'the car wouldn't start' matching 'my vehicle won't turn on' even though they mean the same thing. Embeddings fix that because the model that produces them was trained to put semantically similar text near each other in a vector space, regardless of which exact words were used. On why cosine specifically — it measures direction, not magnitude, and magnitude in these vectors often reflects things like text length rather than meaning, so if you used plain distance, a long irrelevant document could look artificially close to a short, actually-relevant one. Cosine strips that out and focuses on whether the vectors point the same way, which is what the model actually learned to encode. And practically, most embedding models were trained with an objective that's directly optimized around cosine similarity between related pairs, so using it at search time matches how the space was built in the first place — plus, if you normalize the vectors up front, cosine similarity is basically a cheap dot product, which is why it's the default almost everywhere.

questions.title: Choosing a Vector Index Strategy for 500 Million Embeddings
questions.prompt: Your RAG system's vector store has grown from a proof-of-concept size to 500 million embeddings, and exact nearest-neighbor search latency is now unacceptable. Explain the tradeoff between exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search, how an index like HNSW works at a conceptual level, and what you give up by using it.
questions.modelAnswer: Exact nearest-neighbor search computes the similarity between the query vector and every single stored vector, guaranteeing the true top-k results, but the cost scales linearly with the number of vectors — at 500 million embeddings, that brute-force comparison per query becomes too slow for interactive use no matter how well-optimized the dot products are. Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) search trades a small, usually acceptable amount of recall for a large reduction in latency by avoiding a full scan. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each vector is a node connected to its approximate nearest neighbors; the top layers are sparse with long-range links for fast coarse navigation, and lower layers are denser for fine-grained search, so a query starts at the top, greedily moves toward the region of the graph closest to the query vector, then descends layer by layer, refining the search within a progressively smaller neighborhood — this converges to a near-optimal answer in roughly logarithmic rather than linear time relative to the dataset size. What you give up: HNSW is approximate, so it can occasionally miss the true nearest neighbor in favor of a very close one, which is rarely noticeable in a RAG context where top-k retrieval tolerance is already loose; it also has meaningfully higher memory overhead than a flat index because it stores the graph structure alongside the vectors, and build/insertion time is slower than a flat index, which matters for workloads with heavy write volume. The practical decision: for a corpus this size feeding a RAG pipeline where 'close enough, fast' beats 'perfect, slow,' HNSW (or a comparable ANN index like IVF-PQ for even larger, more memory-constrained corpora) is the right tradeoff, with recall validated empirically against a sampled exact baseline rather than assumed.
questions.professionalAnswer: At that scale, brute-force exact search is just not viable anymore — comparing a query against every one of 500 million vectors doesn't fit a real-time latency budget no matter how fast the math is per comparison, because the cost grows linearly with the data. So the move is to an approximate index, and HNSW is the one I'd default to. The way I'd explain it: imagine a graph with a few layers — the top layer has long jumps that get you roughly to the right neighborhood fast, and each layer below that gets denser and more precise, so a search starts coarse and zooms in, which is why it's close to logarithmic time instead of linear. The tradeoff is right there in the name — approximate — so occasionally it'll return the second-best match instead of the actual best, which in a RAG context almost never matters because we're already pulling the top handful of chunks, not relying on one exact match. What I would flag honestly: it costs more memory than a flat index because you're storing the graph on top of the vectors, and it's slower to build and to insert into, so if the use case has heavy write volume, that's a real cost to plan for, not an afterthought. I wouldn't just assume the recall tradeoff is fine — I'd validate it by sampling some queries and comparing ANN results against a brute-force baseline before shipping it.

Describes HNSW only as 'a graph' without the hierarchical layer structure that gives it its speed
Doesn't acknowledge recall loss as a real, if usually small, tradeoff
Omits the memory and insertion-time cost of graph-based indexes versus flat indexes
Doesn't mention validating recall empirically rather than assuming the tradeoff is acceptable

Explains HNSW's hierarchical graph structure and why it achieves near-logarithmic search time

questions.title: Chunking Strategy Is Quietly the Most Important Decision in a RAG System
questions.prompt: Explain why document chunking strategy has such an outsized effect on RAG system quality, compare at least three chunking approaches (fixed-size, sentence/semantic, and recursive/hierarchical), and describe how you'd decide which to use for a corpus of long, structured enterprise policy documents.
questions.modelAnswer: Chunking determines the unit of retrieval, so it directly controls two competing failure modes: chunks too large dilute relevance (the embedding represents an average of many ideas, so a query about one specific clause retrieves a chunk where that clause is buried among unrelated content, and the generator gets more noise alongside the signal); chunks too small lose context (a clause that only makes sense alongside its surrounding definitions or exceptions gets retrieved in isolation, and the generator either hallucinates the missing context or answers incompletely). Fixed-size chunking (e.g., 500 tokens with overlap) is simple and fast to implement and gives predictable embedding costs, but it cuts through sentence and section boundaries arbitrarily, frequently splitting a single idea across two chunks. Sentence or semantic chunking groups text by natural language boundaries or by embedding-similarity breakpoints between sentences, producing more coherent units, at the cost of variable chunk sizes that complicate batching and can still separate a clause from its necessary context if the semantic boundary detector doesn't understand document structure. Recursive/hierarchical chunking respects the document's actual structure — splitting first by section, then by paragraph, then by sentence only if a section is still too large — which is the strongest fit for structured documents like enterprise policies that already have headings, numbered clauses, and defined terms, because it keeps a clause together with its section heading and immediate context by construction rather than by accident. For long, structured policy documents specifically, I'd use recursive/hierarchical chunking anchored to the document's heading structure, attach section-heading metadata to every chunk so retrieval can be filtered or re-ranked by section, and validate the choice empirically with a retrieval-quality eval (does the top-k retrieved chunk actually contain the answer for a labeled set of real questions) rather than picking a chunk size by intuition.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start by naming the actual failure modes, because that's what makes chunking matter so much: chunk too big and you dilute the embedding with unrelated content, so a specific query doesn't retrieve cleanly; chunk too small and you strip away context the answer actually depends on, so the model either guesses or answers half the question. Fixed-size chunking is the easiest to ship but it cuts right through sentences and sections with no awareness of what it's cutting, which is a real problem for policy documents where a clause and its exception might land in two different chunks. Semantic chunking is better because it respects natural breakpoints in the text, but it still doesn't know this is a policy document with headings and numbered sections — it's reading it like prose. For something like enterprise policy docs, I go with recursive, structure-aware chunking: split by section first, then paragraph, then sentence only if a section is still too big, and I attach the section heading as metadata on every chunk so I can filter or boost by section at retrieval time. I wouldn't just pick a chunk size and ship it, though — I'd build a small labeled eval set of real questions with known correct source passages and measure whether the top retrieved chunks actually contain the answer, because that's the only way to know the chunking choice is actually working rather than just looking reasonable.

questions.title: Designing a Forecasting Strategy for Thousands of SKUs, Not Just One
questions.prompt: Your retail client needs demand forecasts for 15,000 SKUs across 200 stores, not one well-behaved national time series. Explain why a single global ARIMA model per series doesn't scale operationally, and lay out the architectural approach you'd take instead, including how you'd decide between local models, a single global ML model, and a hierarchical approach.
questions.modelAnswer: Fitting a separate ARIMA model per SKU-store combination means fitting and maintaining 3 million individual models (15,000 SKUs x 200 stores), each requiring its own stationarity checks, parameter selection, and retraining cadence — this is an operational, not a statistical, problem: monitoring, retraining, and debugging 3 million models individually is untenable, and most low-volume SKU-store combinations don't have enough history for a classical model to estimate parameters reliably anyway, producing wide, unstable prediction intervals. The architectural alternative is a single global machine-learning model (typically gradient-boosted trees or a neural forecasting architecture) trained across all series simultaneously, using SKU, store, and time features (day-of-week, holiday flags, price, promotion indicators, store cluster) as inputs rather than treating each series in isolation — this lets the model borrow statistical strength across similar series, so a new or sparse SKU benefits from patterns learned on similar, higher-volume SKUs, which classical per-series models cannot do at all. The real decision isn't purely binary, though: a hierarchical approach often performs best in practice, reconciling forecasts across levels (SKU-store, SKU-total, store-total, company-total) so that granular forecasts sum consistently to higher-level totals that finance and planning already trust, using a reconciliation method like MinT rather than letting each level disagree with the others. My approach: start with a single global ML model with good features and evaluate it against naive and classical per-series baselines on a representative sample, add hierarchical reconciliation once stakeholders need forecasts to be consistent across aggregation levels (which retail planning almost always does), and reserve local per-series classical models only for the small number of high-volume, well-behaved series where a human forecaster specifically wants to inspect and adjust them.
questions.professionalAnswer: Fitting ARIMA per SKU-store pair sounds reasonable until you do the math — that's 3 million models, each needing its own stationarity check, its own parameter tuning, its own monitoring, and most of those series don't even have enough history to estimate a classical model reliably. That's not a modeling challenge, it's an operations problem that doesn't scale. My default move is a single global model — usually gradient boosting or a neural forecaster — trained across every series at once, with SKU, store, time, and promo features as inputs instead of SKU identity being the whole model. That lets a sparse, low-volume SKU borrow signal from similar SKUs that do have history, which no per-series classical model can do. But I wouldn't stop there, because retail planning almost always needs forecasts that roll up consistently — store totals that actually sum to the company total — so I'd add hierarchical reconciliation on top of the base forecasts rather than letting every level disagree with each other. I'd still keep classical per-series models in my pocket for the handful of high-volume, well-understood series where a human planner wants to see and adjust the model directly, but that's the exception, not the default at this scale.

questions.title: Designing an NLP Classification Pipeline for Millions of Documents a Day
questions.prompt: A client wants to classify support tickets into 40 categories, at a volume of roughly 2 million tickets per day, with a sub-second latency requirement per ticket. Walk through how you'd architect this, including your choice between classical ML (TF-IDF + a linear/boosted model) and a transformer-based classifier, and why.
questions.modelAnswer: At 2 million documents a day with a sub-second per-ticket latency requirement, the decision is driven as much by inference economics as by raw accuracy. A TF-IDF (or similar sparse-feature) representation feeding a linear model or gradient-boosted classifier is extremely cheap at inference — microseconds to low milliseconds per document on CPU — and for a well-defined 40-category taxonomy with reasonable training data per class, it is often competitive in accuracy with a transformer, especially once feature engineering (n-grams, ticket metadata like product line or customer tier) is added. A fine-tuned transformer classifier (e.g., a distilled BERT-family model) typically achieves meaningfully better accuracy on nuanced or ambiguous category boundaries, particularly where the distinguishing signal is semantic rather than keyword-based, but at a real cost: higher per-inference latency and compute, and a GPU or optimized-inference serving layer to hit sub-second latency at this volume without an expensive fleet. My architecture: start with the TF-IDF/boosted baseline because it's cheap to build, interpretable (feature importance maps to actual words, which matters for debugging misclassifications), and establishes a real accuracy floor; evaluate a distilled transformer against that baseline on the actual confusion matrix, specifically looking at which categories the classical model confuses — if those are semantically close categories where a transformer's contextual understanding would plausibly help, that's the justification to invest in the more expensive model; if the baseline's errors are mostly data-quality or ambiguous-ticket issues rather than representational limitations, a transformer won't fix that and isn't worth its cost. If a transformer is justified, I'd serve it through a quantized/distilled model with a batching-aware inference server (ONNX Runtime or TensorRT) to meet the latency SLA at this volume, and keep the classical model as a fast fallback path for degraded-mode operation.
questions.professionalAnswer: At that volume, I'm thinking about cost-per-inference as much as accuracy from the very start. A TF-IDF plus boosted model is nearly free to run — microseconds per ticket on CPU — and for a fixed set of 40 categories with decent training data, it's often good enough, especially once you add ticket metadata as features alongside the text. A transformer classifier will usually do better on the genuinely ambiguous cases where the distinction is about meaning, not just keywords, but it costs real money and real latency at 2 million tickets a day, so I don't reach for it by default. My move is to build the classical baseline first, look specifically at its confusion matrix, and ask: are the errors concentrated in categories that are semantically close to each other, where a model that actually understands context would plausibly do better? If yes, that's my business case for a transformer. If the errors are really about messy or genuinely ambiguous tickets, a fancier model won't fix that, and I'd rather spend the budget on better labeling or ticket intake instead. If I do go with a transformer, I'm not running the full-size model at that volume — I'd distill or quantize it and put it behind an optimized inference server with batching, and I'd keep the cheap classical model running as a fallback path so a spike in traffic or an inference-service issue doesn't take down classification entirely.

Doesn't propose a baseline-first approach to establish whether the simpler model is already sufficient
Uses overall accuracy alone to justify a transformer instead of analyzing where the baseline actually fails

Addresses serving infrastructure needed to meet the latency SLA if a transformer is chosen
Proposes a fallback/degraded-mode path

questions.title: Model Registry Governance: Who Gets to Promote a Model to Production?
questions.prompt: Your organization now has a dozen data scientists registering models in MLflow, but there's no consistent process for what 'production-ready' means, and two incidents have already happened where an unvetted model was promoted. Design the governance process and registry structure you'd put in place.
questions.modelAnswer: The MLflow Model Registry already provides the structural primitives this needs — named registered models, immutable versions, and stage transitions (or, in newer MLflow, aliases/tags replacing the older staging/production labels) — but primitives without process is exactly how you get an unvetted model in production. The governance process I'd put in place: (1) every registered model requires a model card logged as part of its version — training data lineage, evaluation metrics against a held-out set, known limitations, and the owning team — enforced by a CI check that fails registration if required metadata is missing; (2) promotion from 'staging' to 'production' is a gated transition, not a self-service action: require a second reviewer (not the author) to approve against a checklist covering evaluation metrics meeting a defined threshold, a bias/fairness check where relevant, and a rollback plan, implemented via MLflow's webhooks or a wrapper CI/CD pipeline rather than relying on discipline alone; (3) every production promotion is logged with who approved it and why, so an incident retrospective can reconstruct the decision, not just the model's existence; (4) define service-level ownership — a named team or individual is responsible for each production model's monitoring and retraining, registered as a required field, so 'who do we page' is never a post-incident scramble; (5) periodically audit production-stage models against the checklist retroactively, since governance that's only enforced at promotion time decays as models age and their training data drifts further from current reality. The key principle: make the registry the single source of truth for what's actually running in production, and make bypassing the gated process harder than following it, by wiring the gate into the deployment pipeline itself rather than trusting a policy document.
questions.professionalAnswer: The two incidents are the tell that we have the tool but not the process — MLflow's registry already gives us versioned models and stage transitions, but if promotion is just 'anyone can flip a model to production,' that's not governance, that's hope. I'd put a real gate on it: nobody promotes their own model, a second reviewer has to sign off against a checklist — evaluation metrics against a real threshold, documented training data lineage, known limitations, a rollback plan — and that approval gets logged against the model version so if something goes wrong later, we can reconstruct exactly who approved what and why, not just that a model exists. I'd also make sure every registered model has a named owner for monitoring and retraining, because 'whose model is this' turning into a Slack scavenger hunt during an incident is its own failure mode. And I'd wire this into the actual CI/CD pipeline, not a wiki page people are supposed to read, because a policy that relies on everyone remembering to follow it is exactly how we got the two incidents in the first place. Last thing — I'd schedule a periodic audit of what's actually in production against that checklist, because governance that's only checked once at promotion time quietly rots as the data underneath the model drifts.

Doesn't require a second reviewer, relying on the author's self-assessment
Omits logging/audit trail of who approved a promotion and why
Doesn't define ownership for monitoring/retraining of production models
Treats governance as a one-time gate at promotion rather than something requiring periodic re-audit

questions.title: Why a Feature Store Exists: Solving Training-Serving Skew at the Source
questions.prompt: A newer data scientist asks why the team needs a feature store at all when they could just compute features in the training notebook and replicate the logic in the serving code. Explain the real failure mode a feature store prevents, and what you'd actually look for when evaluating whether a feature store is worth the investment for a given team.
questions.modelAnswer: The failure mode a feature store exists to prevent is training-serving skew: when feature logic is written once in a training notebook (often in pandas, batch-oriented, with full historical context available) and then separately reimplemented in serving code (often in a different language, under latency constraints, with only real-time data available), the two implementations drift — a subtly different null-handling rule, a different time-window boundary, a different aggregation that behaves differently on streaming versus batch data — and the model ends up seeing systematically different feature distributions in production than it was trained on, degrading performance in a way that's notoriously hard to detect because nothing throws an error; the model just quietly performs worse. A feature store addresses this by making feature computation a single, versioned, shared definition that both training (via batch/offline retrieval) and serving (via low-latency online retrieval) pull from, so the two paths are structurally guaranteed to agree rather than relying on two engineers keeping two codebases in sync by discipline. It also solves point-in-time correctness for training — ensuring that when you pull historical feature values to build a training set, you get the value as it actually existed at that past timestamp, not a value computed with information that would have leaked from the future. Whether it's worth the investment depends on concrete signals, not enthusiasm: multiple models reusing the same underlying features (duplication risk and skew risk both scale with reuse), a production incident history that traces back to training-serving inconsistency, a real-time serving requirement that makes 'just recompute in the serving code' error-prone under latency pressure, and a team size large enough that informal coordination between training and serving code has already started to break down. For a single data scientist with one model and no real-time serving requirement, a feature store is usually overkill; for an organization running many models sharing overlapping features with a real-time component, it earns its complexity quickly.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd answer with the failure mode, not the feature list, because that's what actually convinces someone. If you write the feature logic once in a notebook and then rewrite it again in the serving service — probably in a different language, under different constraints — those two implementations will drift, and usually nobody notices, because nothing crashes. The model just gets quietly worse because it's seeing features in production that don't match what it was trained on. A feature store's whole value is making that one piece of logic the single source of truth for both training and serving, so there's structurally nothing to drift, instead of hoping two codebases stay in sync by discipline. It also solves a sneakier problem — point-in-time correctness — making sure that when you build a training set from historical data, you're pulling the feature value as it actually existed back then, not one that accidentally uses information from the future. On whether it's worth building: I look for real signals, not vibes — are multiple models sharing the same features, is there a real-time serving requirement that makes 'just recompute it in the service' risky under latency pressure, and has the team actually had an incident that traces back to training-serving mismatch. If it's one person with one model and no real-time path, I'd tell them to hold off — the feature store earns its cost once you've got scale or shared reuse, not before.
